pos: n. pl. (the family of Ozni, a clan of the tribe of Gad)
etymology: Hebrew Ozni, my hearing, or the LORD hath heard, from ozen, an ear; named once, Numbers 26:16.
biblical_def: The Oznites are the family descended from Ozni, fifth son of Gad, and they are named once, in the second census taken on the plains of Moab: “Of Ozni, the family of the Oznites: of Eri, the family of the Erites” (Numbers 26:16). The whole of what Scripture says of this clan is that it existed and was counted. The tribal total follows: “These are the families of the children of Gad according to those that were numbered of them, forty thousand and five hundred” (Numbers 26:18). The purpose of the numbering is given in the chapter itself — the generation that came out of Egypt had died in the wilderness under the LORD's word, and this was the generation that would cross Jordan and receive the land by lot. To be in the list was to have a portion coming. The clan name is a confession: Ozni means that God hears. A household in Gad bore that name through forty years of wandering, and the family was still standing at the end of it, counted among those about to inherit. Gad's men would afterward go over armed before their brethren and win their inheritance east of Jordan only after the west was subdued. The Oznites were part of that company.

corruption_summary: The census lists are read as bureaucratic padding; Numbers 26 is the roll of the generation God brought into the land after burying the one that would not believe.
corruption_paragraphs: A reader who skips Numbers 26 misses the hinge of the book. The first census, in chapter 1, numbered the men who came out of Egypt; this second one numbers their sons, after the carcases of the unbelieving generation had fallen in the wilderness. The list is therefore a record of judgment executed and promise preserved at once. The Oznites are in the second list because God kept a people through forty years of dying, and the counting of them is the proof that He had not abandoned the oath He swore to Abraham.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God numbers His people by household and by name. The modern mind hears a census as depersonalising; Scripture uses it as the opposite — every clan written down, every portion assigned by lot to a named family. The Shepherd who calls His own sheep by name is the God who had the Oznites written into the roll before they ever saw the Jordan.

pos: n. pl. (the family of Jimna, a clan of the tribe of Asher)
etymology: Hebrew Yimnah, prosperity, or whom God keeps back; named once, Numbers 26:44.
biblical_def: The Jimnites are the first-named family of Asher in the census of the plains of Moab: “Of the children of Asher after their families: of Jimna, the family of the Jimnites: of Jesui, the family of the Jesuites: of Beriah, the family of the Beriites” (Numbers 26:44). Asher's total is given three verses on: “These are the families of the sons of Asher according to those that were numbered of them; who were fifty and three thousand and four hundred” (Numbers 26:47). The clan is named and counted and the record moves to the next tribe. Asher was the tribe of oil and of bread: Jacob had said, “Out of Asher his bread shall be fat, and he shall yield royal dainties” (Genesis 49:20), and Moses blessed him with the dipping of his foot in oil. The territory assigned to Asher ran along the coast north of Carmel, and it was country for olives. The Jimnites held a portion in it. Nothing is recorded of this family's deeds, and Asher as a tribe produced no judge and no king; it produced Anna the prophetess, who was in the temple when the infant Christ was brought in, and who spoke of Him to them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem.

corruption_summary: A tribe that produced no ruler is counted a failure; Asher's one named saint in the New Testament was an aged widow who recognised the Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Measured by the standards the world brings to history, Asher is negligible: no judge, no king, no prophet of a book, no great battle credited to it. The Authorized Version records its families, its oil, and its coastline, and then at the opening of the Gospel it records Anna, a widow of fourscore and four years, of the tribe of Aser, who departed not from the temple and who gave thanks when the Lord was presented. That is Asher's portion in the history of redemption, and it is not small.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD's reckoning of a household is not the world's. A clan may be counted once in a census and never mentioned again, and the tribe it belonged to may be remembered chiefly for one old woman's faithfulness in prayer and fasting. The Jimnites were numbered by God, which is the only numbering that finally matters.

pos: n. pl. (the family of Jahleel, a clan of the tribe of Zebulun)
etymology: Hebrew Yachle'el, waiting for God, or hoping in God, from yachal, to wait or to hope, with El, God; named once, Numbers 26:26.
biblical_def: The Jahleelites are the third and last family of Zebulun named in the census: “Of the sons of Zebulun after their families: of Sered, the family of the Sardites: of Elon, the family of the Elonites: of Jahleel, the family of the Jahleelites” (Numbers 26:26). Zebulun's number follows: “These are the families of the Zebulunites according to those that were numbered of them, threescore thousand and five hundred” (Numbers 26:27). The clan's name is a prayer-word: Jahleel means waiting upon God. Zebulun's portion lay in the north, in the hill country that would later be called Galilee of the nations, and it is of that country that Isaiah spoke the prophecy Matthew applies to the ministry of Christ: “The land of Zabulon, and the land of Nephthalim, by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles” (Matthew 4:15). The clan that bore the name of waiting for God held ground on which the Light would afterward dawn. Nothing else is recorded of the Jahleelites; they are a family numbered once. Zebulun itself is commended in Deborah's song as a people that jeoparded their lives unto the death.

corruption_summary: Waiting on God is recast as passivity; the clan named for it belonged to the tribe Deborah praised for jeoparding their lives unto the death.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic religion treats waiting as a mood to be managed and hope as an attitude one generates. Scripture treats waiting on the LORD as an act of the whole man, and it puts the word in the name of a fighting clan. Zebulun, whose third family was called Waiting-for-God, is the tribe of which Deborah sang that they jeoparded their lives unto the death in the high places of the field. Hope in God and hazard of life stand together in the same tribe without strain.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that biblical hope is confident expectation grounded in God's character, not optimism about outcomes. “They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength” is the promise, and the strength is for use. A household named Jahleel in the plains of Moab was waiting for a land it had not seen, and the generation that waited was the generation that crossed.

pos: n. pl. (the Levitical family of Izehar, second son of Kohath)
etymology: Hebrew Yitshar, oil, or anointing oil, from tsahar, to glisten or to shine; named once in this form, Numbers 3:27.
biblical_def: The Izeharites are one of the four Kohathite families of the tribe of Levi: “And of Kohath was the family of the Amramites, and the family of the Izeharites, and the family of the Hebronites, and the family of the Uzzielites: these are the families of the Kohathites” (Numbers 3:27). Their father is named in the same chapter: “And the sons of Kohath by their families; Amram, and Izehar, Hebron, and Uzziel” (Numbers 3:19). The Kohathites held the heaviest charge in the tabernacle service: “This shall be the service of the sons of Kohath in the tabernacle of the congregation, about the most holy things” (Numbers 4:4) — the ark, the table, the candlestick, the altars and the vessels of the sanctuary, carried on the shoulder and never looked upon uncovered. Izehar's house produced both the worst and the best in Israel's worship. Korah, who rose against Moses and Aaron and was swallowed by the earth with his censer in his hand, was the son of Izhar; and the sons of Korah, spared in that judgment, became the singers whose name stands over eleven of the Psalms. The family named for anointing oil bred a rebel against the anointed priesthood and a choir for the house of God.

corruption_summary: Korah's revolt is praised as a democratising of ministry; Numbers 16 names it as presumption against the priesthood God Himself appointed.
corruption_paragraphs: Korah's argument has a long modern career: all the congregation is holy, so why should Moses and Aaron be lifted above the assembly? Egalitarian readings of ministry cite it approvingly, and it is also the standing argument against ordained office in the local church. Numbers 16 answers it by fire and by the earth opening. The LORD had appointed the priesthood; the censers of the rebels were beaten into plates for the altar as a sign to Israel that no stranger should come near. The office is God's to give, and the two offices the New Testament gives the church — elder and deacon — are no more open to self-appointment than Aaron's was.

What the house of Izehar demonstrates is that God's judgment on a rebellion is not His rejection of a family. The sons of Korah did not die with their father, and their descendants were set over the song of the house of the LORD. “Blessed is the man whom thou choosest, and causest to approach unto thee” stands in a psalm of the sons of Korah. The clan named for anointing oil was taught the difference between taking the office and being given a place at the threshold, and it sang about it afterward.

pos: n. pl. (the Levitical family of Uzziel, fourth son of Kohath)
etymology: Hebrew Uzzi'el, God is my strength, from oz, strength, with El, God; named once, Numbers 3:27.
biblical_def: The Uzzielites are the last of the four Kohathite families: “And of Kohath was the family of the Amramites, and the family of the Izeharites, and the family of the Hebronites, and the family of the Uzzielites: these are the families of the Kohathites” (Numbers 3:27). Their chief is named next: “And the chief of the house of the father of the families of the Kohathites shall be Elizaphan the son of Uzziel” (Numbers 3:30). Uzziel was Aaron's uncle, and it was his sons Mishael and Elzaphan whom Moses called to carry Nadab and Abihu out of the camp in their coats after the strange fire consumed them. The house of Uzziel was therefore the house that handled the bodies of the priests who died for offering what God had not commanded, and it did so under the strictest order Aaron ever received, forbidden to mourn. The name means God is my strength, and the family's recorded work was to bear away the evidence of what happens when a man draws near to the LORD on his own terms. In David's day the Uzzielites were still in service: Amminadab the chief of the sons of Uzziel came with a hundred and twelve of his brethren to bring up the ark, after the first attempt had cost Uzza his life.

corruption_summary: The regulative principle is dismissed as rigidity; the house of Uzziel carried out the bodies of the two priests who worshipped God in a way He had not commanded.
corruption_paragraphs: Strange fire is the clearest case in Scripture for the regulative principle of worship, and the modern church has largely decided against it. Nadab and Abihu offered incense the LORD had not commanded them, and fire went out from before the LORD and devoured them. It was Mishael and Elzaphan, sons of Uzziel, who were called to carry them out of the camp. The innovation was not immoral by any ordinary reckoning; it was simply unauthorised, and that was the whole of the charge.

The Reformed and Baptist confessions hold that what God has not commanded in His worship is not permitted, and the Uzzielites are the family that cleared the ground after the point was made. The principle to recover is that acceptable worship is revealed, not devised. The same house was later trusted to carry the ark, and it did so by the appointed order after Uzza had died for touching it on a cart — the Levites bearing it on their shoulders, as the LORD had said.

pos: n. pl. (a family of Kirjath-jearim in the tribe of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Mishra'i, of uncertain sense; taken by some as touching, or spreading out; named once, 1 Chronicles 2:53.
biblical_def: The Mishraites are one of four families reckoned to Kirjath-jearim in the Calebite section of the Judahite genealogy: “And the families of Kirjathjearim; the Ithrites, and the Puhites, and the Shumathites, and the Mishraites; of them came the Zareathites, and the Eshtaulites” (1 Chronicles 2:53). The town itself is traced in the verses above: “These were the sons of Caleb the son of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah; Shobal the father of Kirjathjearim” (1 Chronicles 2:50). Kirjath-jearim is not an obscure place. It was there that the ark of God rested for twenty years after the Philistines sent it back on the cart, in the house of Abinadab on the hill, until David came to fetch it up to Jerusalem. The Mishraites were one of the households of that town — the neighbours of the ark during the long silence between Shiloh and Zion. Scripture records nothing of their deeds. They are named in a register whose purpose was to document which clan held which portion in Judah, and the register preserves them as one of the four families from whom the men of Zareah and Eshtaol afterward came.

corruption_summary: The twenty years of the ark at Kirjath-jearim are passed over; Scripture marks the season as one of lamentation after the LORD, and the families of that town are named.
corruption_paragraphs: Between the fall of Shiloh and the bringing up of the ark to Jerusalem the ark of the covenant sat in a private house on a hill in Judah for twenty years, and Scripture describes Israel's condition in that period in one clause: all the house of Israel lamented after the LORD. It is a period the narrative histories hurry through and the Chronicler documents by household. The Mishraites lived there. The glory had departed from Israel and was lodged, for a generation, among four ordinary clans in a hill town.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is not absent in the long middle. Twenty years with the ark in a borrowed house and no king in Israel looks, from inside, like abandonment; the record shows it as the season in which Samuel judged, the Philistines were subdued at Mizpeh, and the people turned. The clans of Kirjath-jearim were the keepers of the interval.

pos: n. pl. (a family of Kirjath-jearim in the tribe of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Shumathi, of uncertain sense; taken by some from shum, garlic, hence the garlic-growers; named once, 1 Chronicles 2:53.
biblical_def: The Shumathites stand third in the list of the families of Kirjath-jearim: “And the families of Kirjathjearim; the Ithrites, and the Puhites, and the Shumathites, and the Mishraites; of them came the Zareathites, and the Eshtaulites” (1 Chronicles 2:53). Nothing further is recorded of the clan. The verse belongs to the Calebite portion of the Judahite register, which traces the households holding the hill country around Kirjath-jearim, the town where the ark of God remained after its return from the land of the Philistines: “And the men of Kirjathjearim came, and fetched up the ark of the LORD, and brought it into the house of Abinadab in the hill, and sanctified Eleazar his son to keep the ark of the LORD” (1 Samuel 7:1). The Chronicler's interest is tenure — which family held which ground — and the names he preserves are therefore often bare. The Shumathites are such a name. If the derivation from the Hebrew for garlic is right, the clan was known for what it grew, which is the sort of thing neighbours remember and chronicles rarely keep. Scripture kept it.

corruption_paragraphs: Kirjath-jearim was one of the four Gibeonite cities whose men got a covenant from Joshua by craft and were made hewers of wood and drawers of water. Its later households are listed here as families of Judah. The register does not editorialise about their standing; it records them. A clan possibly named for growing garlic sits in the same verse as the town that kept the ark, in the tribe out of which the Lord sprang.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of ordinary labour in a covenant household. Scripture has no category of insignificant work and no reluctance to name a family by its produce. The men who grew food on the hill where the ark rested are in the book, and their inclusion is of a piece with a Saviour known for thirty years as the carpenter.

pos: n. pl. (the men of Zareah, descended from the families of Kirjath-jearim)
etymology: Hebrew Tsar'athi, of Zareah, the place of hornets, from tsir'ah, a hornet; named once, 1 Chronicles 2:53.
biblical_def: The Zareathites are not one of the four families of Kirjath-jearim but a people that came out of them: “And the families of Kirjathjearim; the Ithrites, and the Puhites, and the Shumathites, and the Mishraites; of them came the Zareathites, and the Eshtaulites” (1 Chronicles 2:53). They are the men of Zareah, the town the Authorized Version more often spells Zorah or Zorah's neighbour Zareah in the Shephelah of Judah, on the border toward Dan. The name of the place derives from the hornet, and the hornet is the LORD's own instrument in the conquest: “And I sent the hornet before you, which drave them out from before you” (Joshua 24:12). The settlement of Zareah and Eshtaol by households that had come from Kirjath-jearim is a record of expansion — clans outgrowing one hill town and founding two more. That stretch of country is the country of Samson, whose father Manoah was of Zorah, and between Zorah and Eshtaol is where the Spirit of the LORD began to move upon him. The Chronicler is documenting who held the ground; the narrative books show what happened on it.

And the Spirit of the LORD began to move him at times in the camp of Dan between Zorah and Eshtaol.
corruption_summary: The conquest is read as Israel's achievement; Joshua 24 credits the driving out to the LORD, who sent the hornet before them.
corruption_paragraphs: Israel's entry into Canaan is presented in much modern writing as a military campaign justified after the fact by religion. Joshua's own summary to the assembly at Shechem takes the credit out of Israel's hands entirely: the LORD sent the hornet, and it drove the nations out, and Israel received cities it had not built and vineyards it had not planted. The name of Zareah carries that word for hornet, and the clan that settled there was named after the town.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the land was a gift and not a conquest in the ordinary sense, which is exactly why Israel could forfeit it. The same book that records the hornet records the warning that the LORD who brought them in would scatter them if they turned. The Zareathites held their portion on those terms, and so does every household that holds anything.

pos: n. pl. (one of the ten nations of Canaan promised to Abram's seed)
etymology: Hebrew Qadmoni, easterns, or men of the east, from qedem, the east, or that which is before; named once, Genesis 15:19.
biblical_def: The Kadmonites are named once, in the list of nations whose land the LORD gave to Abram by covenant: “The Kenites, and the Kenizzites, and the Kadmonites” (Genesis 15:19). The covenant itself is in the verse above: “In the same day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, Unto thy seed have I given this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates” (Genesis 15:18). Ten nations are then enumerated, and the Kadmonites are the third. They appear nowhere else in Scripture, under that name, and they are never recorded as having been fought, driven out, or subdued. The name means easterns, and they are generally understood to be a people of the desert east of Canaan — possibly the same stock later called the children of the east. What matters in the text is the form of the transaction. Abram had asked how he should know he would inherit; God answered by cutting a covenant, passing alone between the divided carcases as a burning lamp while Abram slept under a horror of great darkness. The grant was unilateral. The Kadmonites are named in the deed as part of what was given, and their disappearance from the record is no defect in the grant.

scriptures: The Kenites, and the Kenizzites, and the Kadmonites,
In the same day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, Unto thy seed have I given this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates:
And when the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell upon Abram; and, lo, an horror of great darkness fell upon him.
Gen 15:6
And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness.
corruption_summary: The Abrahamic covenant is treated as a bargain with conditions; Genesis 15 shows God alone passing between the pieces while Abram lay in a deep sleep.
corruption_paragraphs: Covenant theology turns on what happened in Genesis 15, and the chapter is handled badly wherever grace is made conditional. In the ancient form of oath, both parties walked between the divided animals, invoking the same fate on themselves if they broke faith. Here Abram is put to sleep and God passes alone, as a smoking furnace and a burning lamp. The obligation is one-sided; the promise does not depend on Abram's performance, and the ten nations listed — Kadmonites among them — are conveyed by the word of God and nothing else.

Two verses earlier stands the sentence Paul builds justification upon: Abram believed in the LORD, and He counted it to him for righteousness. The imputation is reckoned before the covenant is cut and long before the land is entered, which is why Romans 4 can insist that the promise came by faith and not by law. The Kadmonites are a line in a deed whose guarantee is the character of the One who swore it, and that is the pattern of every promise the believer holds.

pos: n. pl. (a people descended from Mizraim, son of Ham)
etymology: Hebrew Lehabim, flames, or the flaming ones, from lahab, a flame or a blade; named twice, Genesis 10:13 and 1 Chronicles 1:11.
biblical_def: The Lehabim are the third people named among the descendants of Mizraim in the table of nations: “And Mizraim begat Ludim, and Anamim, and Lehabim, and Naphtuhim” (Genesis 10:13). The Chronicler repeats the list word for word. Mizraim is the Hebrew name of Egypt, and the peoples listed under him are the nations of the Nile and of Africa northward and westward; the name Lehabim means flames, and is commonly taken as a description of complexion or of the sun-scorched country they held, west of Egypt toward Libya. Nothing else is recorded of them. The table of nations in Genesis 10 is the Bible's own account of how the whole earth was peopled from the three sons of Noah, and it is given before the account of Babel that explains the scattering. Its claim is total: “These are the families of the sons of Noah, after their generations, in their nations: and by these were the nations divided in the earth after the flood” (Genesis 10:32). The Lehabim are one of the seventy, a people whose only memorial is that they came from Mizraim and were counted in the register of the race.

corruption_summary: The table of nations is used to prop up racial hierarchy; Genesis 10 and Acts 17 teach one blood and one origin for every nation on earth.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 10 has been abused in both directions. It was pressed into the service of racial slavery through a false reading of the curse on Canaan, and it is now dismissed altogether as mythic ethnography. Both are refused by the text and by its apostolic use. Paul told the Athenians that God hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and determined their times and the bounds of their habitation. The table of nations is the genealogy behind that sentence: every people in it, the Lehabim included, is kin.

The curse of Genesis 9 fell on Canaan, not on Ham or on his other sons, and it was fulfilled in the Canaanite nations of the land. Mizraim's descendants are listed in the same breath and under no curse at all. The principle to recover is the unity of the human race under one Adam and one Noah, which is the ground both of universal guilt and of a gospel preached to every nation, kindred, tongue and people.
